issues.issue: The instruction that "Student and parent must determine the age of legal competency to sign contracts, in the state of the student's residence" shifts an undefined legal determination to the signers without saying what follows if the determination is wrong. "Minor (under 18 years of age in most states)" is itself hedged and leaves the class of persons who must obtain a parent signature uncertain.

The header requires a parent to sign for a minor "on Parent's behalf and on behalf of the minor student," which must be read against the release in the Agreements of Release paragraph and the binding-effect block, which purport to bind the minor through the parent's signature. Whether a parent's signature can bind the minor's own claims is a point the two passages together leave open.

The definition of "inherent risks" as those "which cannot be eliminated without destroying the unique character of the activities" is a standard whose boundary must be applied case by case, and the list is expressly non-exhaustive ("among others", "some, but not all"). Whether a particular accident was an "inherent" risk is exactly the kind of question a court is asked to construe.

The long enumeration of travel modes and terrain closes with the catch-alls "other means" and "other risks usually associated with such travel," leaving the reach of the disclosed risks against the listed specifics uncertain. Whether a given mishap falls within the enumerated risks or the residual phrase is arguable.

The acknowledgment that staff decisions are "imprecise and subject to errors in judgment" is capable of being read either as a factual disclosure or as an operative allocation of the consequences of instructor misjudgment. That reading matters directly to whether staff negligence is an assumed risk.

As a bullet in the descriptive "Activities and Risks" recital it sits against the operative release, which expressly covers "claims of negligence of a Released Party, but not of gross negligence"; a court may be asked whether instructor misjudgment is an assumed inherent risk or a released negligence claim.

The disclaimer says NOLS has "no responsibility for students during their free time before and after their course," while the first sentence describes free time "before, during and after" the course; by expressio unius, free time during the course is conspicuously omitted from the disclaimer. Whether an injury in mid-course free time is covered turns on that gap, and "free time" is itself undefined.

The statement that staff accompanying students in free time act "as private individuals" for whom NOLS is not responsible is hard to square with the Agreements of Release, which defines "Released Parties" to include staff, employees, volunteers and interns for activities "of NOLS." The two provisions draw the line between NOLS activity and private conduct differently.

The closing sentence that "NOLS field practices in foreign countries are generally consistent with customs and standards used in the United States" reads as an affirmative representation qualified by the vague hedge "generally consistent," whose content cannot be measured. It sits oddly among otherwise purely disclosing risk bullets.

"Private contractors" is illustrated only by transportation ("including, for example"), so the class of persons for whose acts NOLS disclaims responsibility is open-ended. Whether a given service provider is such a contractor rather than "staff" is left to argument.

The disclaimer of responsibility for contractors' acts must be read against the Agreements of Release, whose defined "Released Parties" list (officers, trustees, agents, staff, employees, volunteers, interns) does not include contractors, and against the Decision-Making bullet, which treats contractors' decisions as part of the program. The instrument thus treats contractors as both inside and outside the NOLS program.

The acknowledgment incorporates by reference the Catalog, website, Admission Policies, Enrollment Packet "and other material provided by NOLS describing or related to my program," a catch-all whose reach after the specific list is undefined. What documents form part of the parties' understanding is therefore uncertain.
